A cell s2 refuses even then, or a cell of the grid before the clip that s2 refuses (a grid laid past latitude 90, on which the clip stopped with s2’s message), stops the call with an error of class "spatialkit_cells_degenerate" that names the cells and s2’s reason and says to pass a projected crs or to size the grid by target_cells or n (approx_n_cells in build_tessellation()). The index of the points in a grid laid in degrees gets the same error where s2 refuses a cell.

  • voronoi_seeds_random(), create_grid_polygons_cached() and make_folds(method = "block_kfold", boundary = ) unioned the rows of boundary before repairing them. A boundary that get_voronoi_seeds(), create_grid_polygons() and the tessellation builders repair and use stopped these three with GEOS’s or s2’s bare message: in degrees, a square with a vertex listed twice or a figure eight stopped voronoi_seeds_random() (“Loop 0 is not valid: Edge 1 is degenerate (duplicate vertex)”), with s2 on or off; in a projected CRS, a bowtie row beside a square stopped all three with “TopologyException: side location conflict”. The rows GEOS (in a projected CRS) or s2 (in degrees) refuses are now repaired before the union; valid rows are unioned as they arrived, so a boundary of valid rows gives the seeds, the cache key and the folds it gave. The key of the cache no longer stops on a boundary it cannot union: it then hashes the rows, and create_grid_polygons() gives the outcome it gives uncached.

  • A lon/lat boundary with crossing edges (a bowtie) stopped get_voronoi_seeds(method = "random") and "kmeans", and create_grid_polygons(cellsize = , crs = <geographic>), with s2’s bare “Loop 0 is not valid: Edge 0 crosses edge 2”. In degrees, with s2 on (the default), sf::st_make_valid() is s2’s rebuild, which leaves crossing edges as they are, where GEOS splits them in a projected CRS, so the same boundary ran through create_grid_polygons(target_cells = ) and create_voronoi_polygons(). The rows s2 still refuses after the repair are now rebuilt with crossing edges split, so the seeds and the grid in degrees are placed in the two lobes, as the projected builders place them; voronoi_seeds_random() repairs them the same way. A row s2 refuses even then stops the call with an error of class "spatialkit_cells_degenerate" that names boundary, its rows and s2’s reason, and says to transform boundary to a projected CRS (for the grid, to pass a projected crs or to size the grid by target_cells or n).

  • voronoi_seeds_random() and get_voronoi_seeds(method = "random") and "kmeans" stopped with sf’s bare “sampling box is N times larger than sampling region” on a lon/lat boundary of small pieces far apart. In longitude and latitude sf does not sample a region whose bounding box is over 10,000 times its area, so two small squares on two continents were refused, while the same boundary in a projected CRS was sampled. Such a boundary is now sampled piece by piece: the seeds (or the k-means cloud) are shared among the pieces in proportion to their areas in one draw from the random stream, so they stay uniform over the whole, and each piece is sampled as before. A piece whose own bounding box is over 10,000 times its area stops the call with an error that names boundary and says to transform it to a projected CRS. A boundary sf samples whole gives the seeds it gave.

  • voronoi_seeds_random() and get_voronoi_seeds(method = "random") and "kmeans" exhausted memory on a boundary whose bounding box is far larger than its area. sf draws the points asked for times the ratio of the box to the area in the box and keeps those inside, and the package passed that draw on without a bound. The k-means cloud of two small squares on two continents in a projected CRS, or of a strip 50 km long and 1 m wide at a slant, stopped with R’s “vector memory limit … reached”, and a few random seeds there took most of a minute. A boundary that would take more than 10^6 points drawn in its box (or 10 times the points asked for, if more) is now sampled piece by piece in any CRS, the points shared among its polygons by their areas (or whole, in draws of at most 10^6 points in its box, where that takes less time), and a polygon that would still take more is drawn in such draws. Where the points drawn in all would exceed 2e7 (or 10 times the points asked for, if more), the call stops before any draw with an error that names boundary, the ratio of its box to its area and the points it would take, and says to pass sample_points or ask for fewer seeds. The cloud of the 1 m strip (5e7 points in its box) is refused in this way; the squares on two continents are sampled. A boundary within the first of these limits gives the seeds it gave.

  • A lon/lat boundary with a vertex at a latitude beyond 90 was read as a shape folded over the pole. voronoi_seeds_random() and get_voronoi_seeds() placed seeds 180 degrees of longitude away, a grid laid in degrees put its cells there, clip_target_for() returned a target a few metres high, create_voronoi_polygons() returned 0 cells or stopped with “boundary must be polygonal” on a polygon, and make_folds(method = "block_kfold") said none of the points fell inside boundary, all without saying why. Such a vertex is no place on the Earth, usually metres stamped with a geographic CRS or x and y swapped. These functions, create_grid_polygons(), create_grid_polygons_cached() and build_tessellation() now refuse such a boundary, read as given, with an error of class "spatialkit_cells_degenerate" (site = "boundary") that names its rows and their latitudes and says to check its CRS. A boundary without a CRS that create_grid_polygons(crs =) or build_tessellation(crs =) stamps with a geographic CRS is tested in the same way. A boundary that reaches latitude 90 and not beyond is read as before.

  • A boundary with no polygon that has a location was read in silence or stopped with a bare or false message. A row that is empty, or has a vertex with a coordinate that is not finite or lies beyond 1e150, covers no ground, but clip_target_for() returned a target of area 0 (or 5e204 with a vertex at 1e200), create_voronoi_polygons() returned 0 cells with a warning that blamed the points, the random and k-means seeders stopped with R’s “no applicable method for ‘st_geometry’” or put every seed near y = 1e199, a vertex at Inf moved the cells of the grids, and build_tessellation(method = "hex") and "square" refused a square beside an empty row as “not polygonal”. The readers of boundary (clip_target_for(), create_voronoi_polygons(), build_tessellation(), create_grid_polygons(), create_grid_polygons_cached(), the seeders and make_folds(method = "block_kfold")) now leave such rows out, read as given and again after a move into another CRS, which empties a row it cannot place, so a square beside such a row gives what the square alone gives. A boundary with no row left stops the call with an error that says boundary has no polygon with a location, and why.

  • The random and k-means seeders stopped with R’s “no applicable method for ‘st_geometry’” on a lon/lat boundary whose repair leaves no polygon, and never returned on one whose bounding box has no height. s2 refuses a ring with no height (every vertex on one parallel), and its repair leaves nothing; such a row is now left out like a row without a location, and a boundary with no polygon left stops the call with the error above, whose reason says the repair left no polygon with an area. A ring of three vertices on one parallel is valid under s2, which reads its edges as great circles, but its bounding box has no height, and sf drew in that box without end: voronoi_seeds_random() and get_voronoi_seeds() now refuse a boundary whose bounding box has no height or no width at once, as create_grid_polygons() does.

  • The seeders’ refusal of a lon/lat boundary whose bounding box has no height gave no way forward, and on a boundary sampled piece by piece it said the box of boundary had no height when only one of its polygons had none. In a projected CRS such as the one ensure_projected() picks, a parallel other than the equator is a curve, so a ring with every vertex on it has an area there. The error of voronoi_seeds_random() and get_voronoi_seeds() on such a boundary now says to transform boundary to a projected CRS in which a parallel is a curve, such as the one ensure_projected() picks for it (a polar one, such as EPSG:3413 or 3031, for a ring around a pole), and where only one of the polygons of boundary has a box with no height, it says so. In Web Mercator, World Mercator or plate carree a parallel stays straight and the ring has no area. A ring on the equator or on a meridian holds no ground, and a projected boundary with no height has no area; their errors offer no remedy, as before.

  • The seeders still never returned on most lon/lat rings on a parallel, and on slivers along one. The s2 union of boundary moves the latitudes of such a ring by a few units in the last place, so its box has a height of about 1e-14 degrees and passed the test above, and a sliver 1e-7 degrees tall did the same; which latitudes passed differed between platforms. s2 reads the edges as great circles, which leave the bounding box, and sf (without the lwgeom package) draws in the box and keeps the points in the region, so it drew without end. A lon/lat boundary whose box has less than half its area on the sphere is now refused at once, with the remedy above: in such a box sf drew in less than half the region, so a triangle 120 degrees wide at 80 N, whose box has 0.42 times its area, took seeds only in the part inside the box. With sf_use_s2(FALSE), get_voronoi_seeds() repaired every lon/lat row in the plane, which turned a ring on a parallel into a line and refused it as a row s2 refuses; it now repairs them on the sphere, as with s2 on. voronoi_seeds_random() on a ring along one meridian, whose union on the sphere is a line, returned MULTIPOINT seeds, some empty; it now refuses it, as get_voronoi_seeds() does, with the reason that the union of its rows leaves no polygon with an area, and the reason get_voronoi_seeds() gives no longer says that s2 refuses the row.

  • A boundary row whose repair leaves no polygon made the builders refuse a valid boundary or return a line. A ring with no height (every vertex on one line, or in degrees on one parallel) comes out of the repair of boundary as a line or as nothing. Beside a valid square, build_tessellation(method = "hex") and "square" refused the boundary as “not polygonal”, clip_target_for() returned a target with a line in it, and the grids and Voronoi cells changed; alone, clip_target_for() returned a line and create_voronoi_polygons() returned cells that held none of the points, with a warning that blamed them. Every reader of boundary now leaves such a row out before any move, and again after its own repair, so a square beside it gives what the square alone gives, and a boundary with no polygon left stops the call with the error above.

  • make_folds(method = "block_kfold") stopped with R’s “no applicable method for ‘st_geometry’” on a boundary that is not an sf or sfc layer (a bounding box, a data frame). It now refuses such a boundary by name, as build_tessellation() does.

  • create_grid_polygons_cached() handed a grid returned in degrees to a session with the other sf::sf_use_s2() setting. A grid with a geographic crs and a cellsize is laid in degrees and clipped by s2 with s2 on and by GEOS with s2 off, and ensure_stable_poly_id() rebuilds the cells of a grid returned in degrees that s2 or GEOS calls invalid with s2’s rebuild with s2 on and repairs every cell with GEOS’s with s2 off, so the two settings give two grids. The cache key did not hold the setting, so a call got the grid of whichever setting filled the cache first. The key of a grid returned in degrees now holds the setting, and each setting gets its own entry; every other key is unchanged, so a grid laid and returned in a projected CRS is still found in a cache filled before this change.

  • create_grid_polygons_cached() returned a different grid from create_grid_polygons() for a boundary in degrees with crs given. It projected the boundary to the CRS create_grid_polygons() picks without crs, and the builder then transformed that copy to crs, where the uncached builder transforms the boundary once. The cell counts and IDs agreed, but every corner of the grid differed in the last bits, so no cached cell matched an uncached one on geometry. With crs given the builder is now handed the boundary as the caller gave it, and the cached grid is the one ensure_stable_poly_id(create_grid_polygons()) returns. The same holds for a boundary with no CRS and crs given. The cache keys are unchanged.

  • ensure_stable_poly_id() moved the corners of valid polygons in degrees with s2 on. With make_valid = TRUE (the default), on a layer in longitude and latitude with sf::sf_use_s2() on, every row went through s2’s rebuild, valid or not: valid rows came back with their corners moved by up to 7e-8 degrees and a POLYGON as a MULTIPOLYGON, where with s2 off or in a projected CRS no corner moved. The rows reached the user through create_grid_polygons_cached() with a geographic crs. Only the rows s2 or GEOS calls invalid are rebuilt now, and the other rows are returned as they arrived. The IDs are unchanged.

  • ensure_stable_poly_id() returned rows with crossing edges unrepaired in degrees with s2 on. With make_valid = TRUE (the default), s2’s rebuild does not split crossing edges, so a bowtie, a figure eight or a MULTIPOLYGON whose parts overlap came back invalid under s2 and GEOS, where with s2 off GEOS returns it valid. sf::st_area() then stopped on the row, and its copy in a projected CRS stopped GEOS’s overlay. A row s2’s rebuild leaves invalid is now repaired by GEOS on its coordinates, as with s2 off. Such a row is keyed on that repair, so its ID is the one s2 off gives. With s2 on it was keyed from a second repair that drops the overlap of overlapping parts, and in a layer that holds one, the ID of that row and of its neighbours in the sort order can differ from before. A row GEOS’s repair does not make valid under s2 either, such as a polygon whose edges cross only as great circles, is returned as GEOS repaired it, with a warning that names its rows.

  • ensure_stable_poly_id() said the geometry returned was the caller’s own when it was the repair. When s2 refuses a feature of the lon/lat copy the sort key is measured on, the warning ended “the geometry returned is the caller’s own”. With make_valid = TRUE, the default, the rows returned are the repaired polygons, made in the layer’s own CRS, so a row the repair rewrote came back with another shape than the one given. The warning now says so with make_valid = TRUE, and keeps its words with make_valid = FALSE. No key, ID or row changes.

  • ensure_stable_poly_id(method = "surface_point") passed on sf’s warning about longitude and latitude. The points on the surface are taken on the copy in EPSG:4326 the sort key is measured on, so every call warned “st_point_on_surface may not give correct results for longitude/latitude data” in sf’s words, on any polygon layer moved to that CRS. The key is a sort order in degrees, as ?ensure_stable_poly_id says, and the cell summaries already muffled the same text. The warning is no longer passed on. The points, the IDs and the rows are unchanged.

  • ensure_stable_poly_id() numbered a layer far from its CRS’s origin by the row order. PROJ returns a row of a projected layer it cannot move to the sort CRS (EPSG:4326 by default) as an empty row, or a ring without the vertices it cannot place, instead of stopping. A UTM layer shifted by 1e8, 1e12 or 1e15 then had a NaN key for every row, and its IDs followed the row order, so the same polygon took another ID when the rows came in another order; with method = "surface_point" and a ring left with two vertices the call stopped with GEOS’s “Invalid number of points in LinearRing”. create_grid_polygons_cached() numbered its cells the same way at such offsets. A move that cannot place every polygon with a location now takes the documented fallback a failed move takes: the whole layer is sorted in its own CRS, and the log says so. A move that stops no longer passes on GDAL’s warning beside that log line. A key in a CRS that is not geographic (this fallback, a layer without a CRS, transform_for_sort = NULL or a projected sort CRS) is now rounded to a step that grows with the magnitude of the coordinates: the power of two at or above 2^-44 of the layer’s largest, never under 1e-7 of its unit, with ties ordered at the step of each polygon’s own largest coordinate. Cells 1e12 m out were ordered by the last bits of their centres, so a hex grid took other IDs there than at the origin, with or without a CRS. A layer within about 1.7e6 units of its origin is still rounded to 7 decimals. A feature whose point or area the sort copy cannot give is keyed by the centre of its box with area 0, as an empty polygon is, where the call stopped with GEOS’s message. A ring of fewer than four points encloses no area and is dropped from the key and from the repair: GEOS stopped the repair on a ring of two (“Invalid number of points in LinearRing”), and in degrees sf read such a ring as the whole globe and every call stopped with “To set the crs to NA, first remove the full polygons”. A polygon left with no ring is keyed by the centre of the box of its points. Layers keyed in degrees get the IDs they got; a layer keyed in its own unit beyond about 1.7e6 units from its origin gets other IDs only where two centres lie within the new step of each other.

  • ensure_stable_poly_id(make_valid = TRUE) returned rows its repair turned into lines. GEOS’s repair gives an empty polygon back as LINESTRING EMPTY, and a ring with no area (every vertex at one latitude, or on one line) as a GEOMETRYCOLLECTION of lines or an empty one, and those rows came back in a layer given as polygons, without a word. An empty polygon is no longer repaired and comes back as it arrived. A row the repair leaves with no polygon, a row of rings of fewer than four points among them, comes back as it arrived, with one warning of class spatialkit_cells_degenerate that gives its rows of polygons_sf; a row the repair turns into a collection keeps its polygonal parts. Valid layers come back as they did.

  • Cells built on seeds placed from lon/lat points could leave observations near the edge of a wide layer in no cell. The seeding functions attach the convex hull of the points they cluster as the seeds’ cover, and build_tessellation() and create_voronoi_polygons() move the cover into the CRS the cells are built in with its edges read as straight lines in degrees, then grow it by 2 percent of its diagonal. For points in a geographic CRS the hull was the one sf builds with s2, whose edges are great circles, and away from the equator a great circle bows toward the pole. Of 800 points uniform over the box of the conterminous United States, 24 lay outside the hull read in degrees; one of them, near the northern edge, lay 130 km outside it in the cells’ CRS against a margin of 127 km, and fell in no cell at 44 and at 178 seeds. assign_features_to_polygons() said so (spatialkit_unassigned), and the summary of the cells built on a selection’s seeds then raised spatialkit_cells_differ. Round a pole the hull, read in degrees, held few of the points: of 600 points north of 70 degrees, 230 fell in no cell at 10 seeds, where it held none of the seeds and was set aside with spatialkit_no_cover, and 17 at 60 seeds, where it was used. For points spread round the globe it was the whole sphere, and was set aside too. For points on both sides of 180 degrees, read in degrees, it ran the long way round the globe: between 170 E and 170 W and 45 S and 45 N the cells on 10 seeds were 11 times the area of the points’ hull, and of 600 points between 105 E and 105 W and 20 N and 70 N, 239 fell in no cell at 10 seeds. The hull is now taken on the coordinates in degrees, as it already was with sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE) and for points with no CRS, and for points on both sides of 180 degrees with their longitudes taken from 0 to 360 (-170 as 190), the short way round. Where the cells are built in a CRS that splits the map at 180 degrees, as Web Mercator, the CRS for points spread round the globe, does, a cover whose longitudes run past 180 is cut there into two pieces, one at each side of the map. On all these layers every observation now has a cell, and between 170 E and 170 W the cells are 1.3 times the points’ hull. attr(, "cover") of seeds placed from lon/lat points is now that hull, and its longitudes run past 180 for points on both sides of 180; s2 reads its edges as great circles, so tested against it with s2, points near a long edge can lie outside it. Cells on such seeds can differ at their outer edge, and differ throughout where the cover was set aside or ran the long way round. Layers in a projected CRS, seeds drawn in a boundary and the hull a profile keeps are unchanged.

  • A selection by size called the default size the caller’s choice. On a default call, where nothing names a size, select_resolution()’s note read “the count is set by obs_per_cell = 4.5, the caller’s choice; no criterion chose it.” It now reads “obs_per_cell = 4.5, the default” whenever the size is 4.5, and “the caller’s choice” for any other size, which only a caller gives, to the selection or to the profile. ?select_resolution and vignette("resolution") said that the count of a selection by size stands “since the caller set it”; they now say that it stands since a size set it and no criterion.

  • The print of attr(, "pooled") hid the fit of a column whose tau2 is 0. summarize_by_cell() fits such a column, and every pooled value is then its neighbours’ mean, but the print showed only “status : no signal between cells”, also for a response whose cells predict a left-out row better than one mean, and listed the column’s interval under “Also in the frame” as if it belonged to nothing above. The block is now printed in full (value, variances, own weight, the leave-one-out errors and the interval), with a line that tau2 is 0, every own weight is 0 and each value is its neighbours’ mean. Whether the cells do better than one mean is said on the loo line, as for any other column. The status in the record, and the warning, are unchanged.

  • The warning spatialkit_pool_few_cells did not say when the pooled values of two cells change places. With 2 to 9 cells a cell’s target is the mean of every row outside it, so the overall mean lies between the target and the cell’s own mean, and a cell whose own weight is below its share of the column’s rows gets a pooled value on the far side of the overall mean. With two cells and tau2 at 0 every own weight is 0, and each cell’s pooled value is the other cell’s mean. The warning said only that a cell “with a small own weight” crosses the overall mean and that two cells can change order. It now gives the share of the column’s rows as the bound, and names each column with two cells and tau2 at 0, whose two values change places. The “Conditions” entry of ?summarize_by_cell says the same; its “Pooled values” section already did. The values and the condition’s fields are unchanged: such a column has cells 2 and own_weight 0.

  • On gridded locations the pooling’s neighbours depended on the unit and the origin of the coordinates. A cell’s 8 neighbours are the cells whose centroids are nearest, and a tie between two goes to the lower x, then the lower y. Only exact ties counted: centroids of cells on a lattice tie exactly in one unit and differ in their last bits in another, so the same layer in metres and in feet, or with the origin moved, gave some cells other neighbours, and since tau2 is fitted over the layer every pooled value of summarize_by_cell() moved, and so did the leave-one-out error of resolution_profile() on the same cells. The nearest other location of a row alone in its cell, which the error of a plain mean reads, had the same fault. Two squared distances within one part in ten million of each other are now a tie, coordinates within that part of the distance count as equal, and of cells still tied the one of the lower number is taken (in summarize_by_cell(), the one whose ID sorts first), so the same cells in another unit or with another origin get the same neighbours and the same values, cells whose centroids coincide among them. That holds while the spacing of the lattice is above about a ten-millionth of its coordinates. Where three to eight cells’ centroids coincide the values agree to rounding. Layers without such ties are unchanged. Another projection still gives other distances.

  • Where more cells’ centroids shared a point than a cell has neighbours, which of them each took depended on the unit and the origin of the coordinates. A cell whose centroid shares its point with 8 other cells or more takes the first 8 of them by ID, without a search. The point was found by exact equality. In another unit, or with the origin moved, rounding parts such centroids by a few units in the last place, and the cells were then searched for among themselves by those distances. Twelve cells of 1 to 12 rows on one point beside a 10 by 10 lattice of one-row cells at 250 m gave 3 cells other neighbours in feet and 12 with the origin moved by 0.1 m. Since tau2 is fitted over the layer, every pooled value of summarize_by_cell() could move, by up to 0.21 on that layer, and so could the leave-one-out error of resolution_profile() on the same cells. Centroids that lie within a ten-millionth of the largest coordinate of one another, in x and in y, now count as one point; that is the reach of the tie rule above. Where other centroids that close chain on further than that, the chain is taken again at half the reach, and so on, until its parts span no more than the reach they were taken at. Such cells take the same neighbours, and get the same values, in another unit and with the origin moved by little against the coordinates. Cells whose centroids lie that close without coinciding take each other by ID too, not by distance. The reach follows the largest coordinate, so with the origin moved far, to the corner of the data say, such centroids can lie beyond it and their cells then take the nearest. A layer whose centroids are either equal or further apart than that reach in x or in y gets the same neighbours and values as before.

  • On gridded locations the density partition depended on the unit and the origin of the coordinates. The regions resolution_profile(), get_voronoi_seeds() and voronoi_seeds_kmeans() draw under partition = "density", and with them rss, loo and the count chosen, differed between metres and feet, or with the origin moved by 0.1 m: on a 40 by 30 lattice at 250 m the default profile gave loo 0.2978 in EPSG:26915, 0.3068 in UTM 15N in US feet and 0.3006 with the false origin moved. On a lattice many distances tie exactly, and the last bits of the coordinates, which move with the unit and the origin, settled them in four places: the neighbour searches of the density weights and the nearest-centre search of Lloyd’s iteration counted exact ties alone; the first k-means++ centre was drawn from weights equal but for their last bits, which sample.int() reads as different; the locations, which the random draws index, were put in order by first coordinates equal but for their last bits; and of two starts whose sums agree to rounding, the rounding chose. Now squared distances within one part in ten million of each other are a tie in those searches, as in the pooling’s: a tie between neighbours goes to the lower first coordinate, then the lower second, and a tie between centres to the lower-numbered one. The first centre is drawn on the weights with those within one part in ten million of each other made equal, first coordinates within that part of the extent count as equal when the rows and the locations are put in order (so a profile that draws a subsample of the rows draws the same locations in every frame), and a later start is kept only when its sum is lower by more than that part. The regions are the same in another unit or with another origin as long as no coordinate moves by more than about a two-hundred-millionth of the distance between neighbouring locations; coordinates rounded more coarsely can still give other regions. The lattice above gives loo 0.3066 and the same regions in all three. The scoring of a profile’s levels, the refit of select_resolution(), the edge rule of assign_features_to_polygons() and cell_values_at() take the same tie between centres, so a row the profile scores in the cell of the lower-numbered of two tied centres is assigned there too: for such a row the assignment’s margin also takes in its distance from the boundary of the two cells, which midway between centres far apart can exceed one part in 1e10 of the coordinates. Layers on which no two distances, no two weights, no two first coordinates and no two starts’ sums come within one part in ten million of each other are partitioned as before; on others the regions, and every figure drawn from them, can differ from before for the same seed. resolution_profile() puts the rows in this order under partition = "kmeans" too, so there a layer with two first coordinates that close can also get other regions for the same seed.

  • On gridded locations the k-means partition depended on the unit and the origin of the coordinates. The regions resolution_profile(), get_voronoi_seeds() and voronoi_seeds_kmeans() draw under partition = "kmeans", the refit of such a profile by select_resolution() and the sweep of determine_optimal_levels() differed between metres and feet, or with the origin moved by 0.1 m: on a 40 by 30 lattice at 250 m the default profile under partition = "kmeans" gave loo 0.2963 in EPSG:26915, 0.2998 in UTM 15N in US feet and 0.3000 with the false origin moved, and voronoi_seeds_kmeans(k = 40, partition = "kmeans") put 391 and 363 of the 1,200 points in other cells. stats::kmeans() (Hartigan and Wong) settles a tie between two centres by the last bits of the coordinates, which move with the unit and the origin, and it takes no tolerance. It is now handed the coordinates centred on the middle of their bounding box, divided by its diagonal and rounded to 2^-30 of it (about a billionth). The starts are drawn from those coordinates and the best start is chosen by its sum on them. Distinct locations that would round to one point keep their coordinates unrounded, so distinct locations stay distinct and stats::kmeans() refuses no count the callers allow. The cells come back in the order of the rows given, and the centres, the within-cell sums of squares and every figure read off the cells are taken in the layer’s own coordinates. The seeding functions with init = "kmeans++" and determine_optimal_levels() put the rows in order as resolution_profile() does, first coordinates equal but for their last bits counting as one column. The lattice above gives the same regions in all three. stats::kmeans() also settles ties by the last bits of its own compiled arithmetic, which differ between platforms, so on a layer where ties decide cells the regions, and every figure read off them, can differ between platforms for the same coordinates and seed: this lattice gets other regions on Linux on x86-64 than on macOS on arm64. A change of unit or origin can still move a coordinate across the middle of a rounding step, and does so more often the smaller the extent: over 60 lattices, each in five other units or origins, the regions were the same on every lattice that spans a kilometre or more and differed in 205 of 1,560 partitions of lattices that span less (“The partition” in ?resolution_profile). On layers where no tie decides a cell the regions are those of earlier versions, and the centres and sums of squares differ from before in their last bits; where two starts reach the same regions with sums equal to rounding, the start kept can be the other one, so the centres, the seeds and the cells numbered by them can come in another order. On gridded locations the regions, and every figure drawn from them, can differ from before for the same seed.

  • The count of distinct locations that caps the ladders and the seeds depended on the unit of the coordinates. resolution_profile() (its support ceiling, under both kinds), determine_optimal_levels() (the top of its ladder) and get_voronoi_seeds() and voronoi_seeds_kmeans() (the most seeds they return) counted the distinct locations after rounding the coordinates to 8 or 10 decimals of the layer’s unit. Forty locations, each listed twice 2e-8 m apart, counted 80 in metres and 40 in UTM 15N in kilometres: the profile’s ladder stopped at 40 cells in kilometres and at 79 in metres, voronoi_seeds_kmeans(k = 79) returned 58 seeds in kilometres and 79 in metres, and determine_optimal_levels() returned other counts. The locations are now counted on the coordinates stats::kmeans() is handed (centred, divided by the diagonal of their bounding box and rounded to 2^-30 of it, distinct locations kept distinct), so the count is the same in every unit: 80 in metres, in kilometres and in US feet. Locations closer than 1e-8 of the layer’s unit (1e-10 for the seeds) could count as one and now count as distinct, so such a layer can get a higher ceiling and more seeds than before.

  • predict_surface() took a grid point’s covariates from whichever of several equally near features of covariates GEOS met first, so the surface moved with the unit and the origin of the coordinates. A grid laid between the points of a lattice is the same distance from four of them, and sf::st_nearest_feature() settled the tie by the last bits of the distances. On a 20 by 15 lattice at 250 m, with the grid at the midpoints, 147 of 266 grid points took another covariate row in UTM 15N in US feet than in EPSG:26915, and 189 with the false origin moved by 0.1 m; .pred moved by up to 0.03. For point covariates, squared distances within one part in ten million of the least, plus a margin, are now a tie, and the tie goes to the point lowest in x (x values within one part in ten million of the diagonal of the points’ bounding box, or within one part in 1e10 of their largest coordinate where that is more, counting as one), then lowest in y (y values read the same way), then first in row order. The grid above takes the same covariates in all three frames, with or without the FNN package. Two points that differ only in the last bits of their coordinates (one station recorded twice, one billionth of a metre apart) now take the tie the same way with another origin, where a grid point the same distance from both, 570 m away, took one row in metres and US feet and the other with the false origin moved by 0.1 m; the first in row order takes it now, and so does a grid point near the pair, however near (see the entry on a point a hair from two records of one station). A grid point that ties with no other point takes the row it took before. Lines and polygons had the same fault: a grid point on the edge two covariate polygons share, or at the shared end of two lines, is at distance 0 from both, and GEOS gave it either. On 10 by 8 square cells of 500 m with the grid on their shared edges, 34 of 72 grid points took another cell with the false origin moved by 0.1 m, and 29 with the rows of covariates shuffled. Distances within one part in ten million of the least, plus one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of covariates, are now a tie, and the tie goes to the feature whose bounding-box centre is lowest in x, then lowest in y (x values and y values within one part in ten million of the diagonal of the bounding box of covariates counting as one), then first in row order: each of the 72 takes the cell to its left in every frame and row order. Features whose box centres all coincide (a polygon with a hole and the island that fills it, alone in the layer, the polygon first) now take the tie the same way with another origin, where a grid point on the hole’s ring took the polygon in metres and US feet and the island with the false origin moved by 0.1 m. A grid point with one nearest feature takes the row it took before. Layers in degrees are searched as before. ?predict_surface (covariates) states the rule. A point of a grid kept as given with a coordinate that is not finite or lies beyond 1e150 now gets NA covariates, whatever the layer, where it took those of a row GEOS gave it. With point covariates its .pred was NA as well; with lines or polygons, or with a layer in degrees, it got a finite .pred from that row where ?predict_surface (grid) states NA, and now gets NA.

  • A point a hair from two records of one station took the nearer record by the last bits of the coordinates, which move with the unit and the origin. The nearest-centre search of predict_surface() (point covariates), cell_values_at() (the nearest scored location, seed or centre), resolution_profile() (the cell of each scored row and the steps of the density partition), make_folds() ("knndm"), assign_features_to_polygons() (a point on the edge between two cells a profile scored) and get_voronoi_seeds() (the seeds of a selection) counted two centres as a tie when their squared distances agreed to within one part in ten million. Two records one billionth of a metre apart have squared distances from a point r away that differ by about 2r times that billionth, within one part in ten million of r^2 only while r is more than about 2 cm. Closer, the nearer by the last bits was taken: of 320 grid points 0.1 mm to 2 cm from such a pair, 48 to 60 took another covariate row in UTM 15N in US feet or with the false origin moved by 0.1 m than in EPSG:26915, and cell_values_at() filled 20 of 160 locations 1 mm from the station from another cell. A squared distance now ties with the least when it is no more than the square of the least distance lengthened by a margin, plus one part in ten million of the least squared distance. The margin is one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the centres, at most a millionth of the diagonal of their bounding box and at least four times the spacing of doubles at that coordinate, as for the lines and polygons of covariates. No grid point and no location of those layouts moves between the frames. A point whose two nearest centres differ in distance by less than the margin, and that took the nearer, now takes the lower-numbered one (for predict_surface() and cell_values_at(), the one their column order puts first). The margin grows with the largest coordinate, as that of lines and polygons does: about 0.46 mm at a UTM northing near 4,550 km, about half a micrometre once the origin lies next to data 5 km across. A point whose distances to two centres differ by less than the margin with one origin and by more with another takes the lower-numbered centre with the first and the nearer with the second, in the searches above that work in the layer’s own coordinates (the k-means steps of the density partition and of "knndm" run in a frame centred on the data and do not). ?predict_surface, ?cell_values_at, ?resolution_profile, ?make_folds, ?summarize_by_cell and ?assign_features_to_polygons state the rule.

  • The attr(, "kmeans") record of get_voronoi_seeds() for the scored centres of a profile or selection gave a point the same distance from two seeds to whichever sf::st_nearest_feature() returned, so cluster, size and withinss moved with the unit and the origin, and could differ from the cells the profile scored. On a 40 by 30 lattice at 250 m with the 267 centres of resolution_profile(seed = 1), cluster differed from the one in EPSG:26915 in 5 rows in UTM 15N in US feet and in 2 with the false origin moved by 0.1 m, and in each frame 1 to 4 rows were not in the cell the profile scored them in. Each point now goes to its nearest seed by the profile’s rule: squared distances within one part in ten million of the least are a tie, and a tie goes to the lower seed_id. The record then holds the profile’s cells in every frame, and tot_withinss scales with the square of the unit. ?get_voronoi_seeds states the rule.

  • build_tessellation() let the unit and the origin of the coordinates choose the cell of a lattice point on a cell edge, and of a point snapped to two cells the same distance away. A point on the edge two cells share went to the smaller cell_id only while the edge passed through the point exactly; the last bits of the coordinates put it a hair inside one cell or the other. On a 40 x 30 lattice at 250 m with square cells of 1000 m, 80 of 1200 rows were in another cell in UTM 15N in US feet than in EPSG:26915 and 226 with the false origin moved by 0.1 m; with hexagons, 156 with the origin moved. A point within a margin of one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the cells from a cell’s edge is now in that cell, and a point in two or more cells takes the smallest cell_id. A point just outside every cell, snapped to the nearest cell, went to whichever cell sf::st_nearest_feature() returned when two were the same distance away: of 180 points beside the corners of boundary cells, 4 to 27 went to another cell in US feet, international feet, kilometres and with moved origins. Among the cells as near to one part in ten million it now goes to the smaller cell_id. The index is the same in every frame on both layers. params$snapped no longer lists a point within the margin of an edge, which is in that cell. The same index serves create_voronoi_polygons() and the check of a cover. ?build_tessellation (index) states the rule.

  • build_tessellation(method = "triangles") split the squares of a lattice by the last bits of the coordinates. The four corners of each square lie on one circle, and qhull split the square by the rounding of the coordinates it was handed, which moves with the unit and the origin. A 37 x 25 lattice at 250 m gave 1728 triangles in EPSG:26915 and in UTM 15N in US feet, 860 of them other triangles in US feet, and 1827 with the false origin moved by 0.1 m, 99 of them flat. qhull, and GEOS where the geometry package is not installed, are now handed the points centred on the middle of their bounding box, divided by its diagonal and rounded to 2^-30 of it, and each triangle is drawn on the points’ own coordinates. The lattice gives the same 1728 triangles in every frame, none flat, but where a point lies within its own rounding noise of the middle of such a step. A jittered lattice gives the triangles it gave. ?build_tessellation says so.

  • create_voronoi_polygons() and build_tessellation(method = "voronoi" | "triangles") merged near-coincident points by ten decimals of the layer’s unit, so the number of cells moved with the unit and the origin. 60 points with copies of 20 of them moved by 3e-8 m gave 80 cells in metres and 65 in kilometres; moved by 1e-9 m, 80, 62, 79 and 60 cells in metres, in US feet, with the false origin moved by 0.1 m and in kilometres. With keep_duplicates = FALSE points are now merged when they round to one point in coordinates centred on the middle of their bounding box, divided by its diagonal and rounded to 2^-30 of it, so points within about a billionth of the extent of each other count as coincident in any unit or origin: both sets of copies give 60 cells in every frame. Points that close but more than ten decimals of the unit apart, which were kept, can now be merged: copies 1e-6 m apart on that 5 km layer gave 80 cells and give 64. ?create_voronoi_polygons and ?build_tessellation (keep_duplicates) said the argument had no effect, which was false for points that close; they now say what each value merges.

  • create_grid_polygons(cellsize = ) laid an extra row or column of sliver cells over a boundary whose side is a whole number of cells, in some units and origins. sf counts the cells per side as ceiling(width / cellsize), and rounding put a 9000 m side at 9.0000000000001741 cells of 1000 m with the false origin moved by 0.1 m. The square grid had 60 cells there against 54 in EPSG:26915 and in UTM 15N in US feet, the smallest of 5e-8 m^2, and the hexagonal grid 79 against 76. A side that exceeds a whole number of square cells by no more than a margin of one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the boundary now gets that number, the side target_cells derives as well, and with clip = TRUE a cell that meets the boundary only within that margin of its edge is dropped. The grids above have 54 and 76 cells in every frame. build_tessellation(method = "square") on a 37 x 25 lattice at 250 m in its own box gave 70 cells with the origin moved against 54, and approx_n_cells = 54 gave 63; both give 54 in every frame, and so does create_grid_polygons_cached(). A side more than that margin over a whole number keeps its row or column of narrow cells, however many cells it holds, as before. ?create_grid_polygons (cellsize, clip) states the rule.

  • cell_values_at() without seeds settled a tie between two scored locations of one lattice column by their exact x, so the fill from the nearest scored location moved with the origin. Of two locations of one column the same distance from a location asked for, the one whose x was lower in its last bits won, and a lattice moved to another false origin no longer has one x per column. On a 20 x 15 lattice at 250 m, 2 of 14 locations midway between two points of the first column took the upper point with the false origin moved by 0.1 m, where EPSG:26915 and US feet take the lower, and their filled_from and value moved with it. The scored locations are now in column order (x values within one part in ten million of the diagonal of their bounding box, or within one part in 1e10 of their largest coordinate where that is more, counting as one), then in row order (y values read the same way), then by the first cell in ID order among their rows, so the tie goes to the lower point in every frame, as “Ties” in ?cell_values_at said of another unit or origin. Two scored locations that differ only in the last bits of their coordinates (one station recorded twice, in two cells) now take the tie the same way with another origin, from the cell first in ID order as rows at one location do, where the fill came from one cell in metres and US feet and from the other with the false origin moved by 0.1 m. That section now states the column rule.

  • summarize_by_cell() read columns at extreme scales as having no spread. The test compared the spread inside the cells with the size of the values, so 1e15 plus a spread of 1 was called constant, and so were values near 1e200 and 1e-170, whose squares overflow and underflow. The warning said their values “do not vary inside any cell”, and the pooled values were the plain means. The test now also reads the column centred on its median and scaled by its largest distance from it, and a column has no spread only where neither reading finds any. On that column a standard deviation, over all the rows or inside the cells, of at most three units in the last place of the column’s largest absolute value is rounding: a column whose values differ only by their rounding (0.1 beside 0.3 / 3, 2 beside sqrt(2)^2) has no spread by either reading, as before, while 1e15 plus a spread of 1, at eight such units, has spread. Where the raw values lose their spread to rounding, the fit is made on the scaled column and put back in the column’s units: for 1e15 plus a spread of 1 the weights, sigma2, tau2 and the leave-one-out errors are those of the spread alone, and the pooled values are those of the spread plus 1e15, to the rounding of a value stored at 1e15. The warning for no spread inside any cell now says the values do not vary there “to the precision of the values”. A column that is not constant, with an absolute value above 1e150 or a largest distance from its median below 1e-150, gets NA pooled columns, with a spatialkit_pool_unavailable warning whose reason is "values out of range", and its plain columns are returned: beyond these bounds the squares of many values can overflow or lose their precision. A few columns just beyond them were still fitted and are now refused: at 800 rows, 1e150 to 1e152 times a spread of 1, and 1e-151 to 1e-160 times a spread of 1. Inside the bounds, every column whose raw values show their spread gives the numbers it gave, except the standard errors of the leave-one-out errors (loo_se in the record and in resolution_profile()), which square the squares: for residuals above about 1e77 they were Inf, and below about 1e-80 they lost their precision and then were 0. They are now taken on the residuals divided by a power of two. resolution_profile() reads its estimate’s columns the same way: attr(, "estimate")$constant and loo_one_cell follow the engine’s test, so loo is computed for 1e15 plus a spread of 1, and values beyond those bounds leave loo, loo_se and own_weight NA at every level with the same warning; print(), summary() and select_resolution(criterion = "loo") of such a profile say why. At values beyond the bounds the test of a constant response for cp (attr(, "one_cell")$constant) finds the response constant, one spatialkit_pool_unavailable warning names cp, moran_i and moran_z as well, and summary() says the values are out of range rather than constant. The test for cp now reads the values the same way as the estimate’s (see the entry on a response at a large offset).

  • summarize_by_cell(deff = "kish") called a column in small units constant. The ICC skipped a column as one that does not vary when its standard deviation was below .Machine$double.eps (about 2.2e-16), whatever the size of its values. A column that varies, in units that make its values of order 1e-16 or smaller, got an ICC of NA with the reason “the column does not vary”, no design effect and the uncorrected standard errors, without a warning, while the same column in larger units got its correction: on 800 points in 178 cells the ICC was 0.478 at a scale of 1 and of 1e-14 and NA at 1e-17, where the standard errors came out 2.2 times smaller. Where only the rows with a cell id were that small, the ICC was NA with “its values differ only on rows that fall in no cell”, and its standard errors NA. Where the standard deviation is below that floor or not finite, the column is now read again centred on its median and scaled, as for the pooled values, and it does not vary only where neither reading finds spread; a column with spread gets its ICC from the scaled column, which is the ICC of the column. A column whose values are all equal still has an ICC of NA and standard errors of 0. A column whose values differ only by their rounding (0.1 beside 0.3 / 3) still has an ICC of NA with “the column does not vary”; its standard errors are 0 in a cell whose values are equal, and of the size of that rounding in a cell whose values differ. Such a column was read that way only while its standard deviation was below the floor: the same values multiplied by 16 or more, whose rounding is above it, got an ICC of 0.395 from that rounding and a design effect on their standard errors, while the pooled summary of the same call said the column does not vary. Now the column is also read again where its sum of squares shows no spread on the scale of its values, so a column that differs only by its rounding does not vary at any size. A column whose standard deviation overflows, with values near 1e200, had an ICC of NA with “the variance decomposition is undefined”; its ICC is now estimated. Columns with spread whose standard deviation is finite and at or above the floor give the ICC they gave.

  • summarize_by_cell() gave standard errors of NA or 0 in silence for a column in very large or very small units. The standard deviation inside a cell squared the deviations of the raw values from the cell mean. For values above about 1e154 the squares overflowed, and in each cell where they did ..sd_* was Inf and the standard errors and intervals were NA, under any deff, with no warning. For a spread below about 1e-154 the squares lost their bits, and at a spread of 1e-170 ..sd_* and the standard errors were 0, which says that the mean has no error. Where the raw standard deviation is not finite or is below 1e-150, it is now taken on the cell’s values centred on their median and divided by powers of two, so ..sd_*, ..se_* and the intervals of a column follow its unit. A cell whose standard deviation is beyond the largest double (a spread of order 1e308) still has ..sd_* of Inf and standard errors of NA, now with a warning of class "spatialkit_sd_overflow" that names the columns and gives the number of such cells of each (fields columns and cells). Every other standard deviation is the one it was.

  • estimate_sac_range() and the test for cp in resolution_profile() called a response at a large offset constant. Both read the raw values alone. estimate_sac_range() refused a response whose standard deviation is under 1e-12 of its largest absolute value, so 1e15 plus a spread of 1, eight units in the last place of its values, was “the response is constant” and, with predictor_vars, “the residuals on predictor_vars are constant: the predictors explain the response exactly”. The profile left cp, moran_i and moran_z NA at every level while it scored loo, and select_resolution(criterion = "cp") refused. Where the raw values show no spread, both now read them again, as summarize_by_cell() does: a response has spread when, centred on its median and scaled, its standard deviation is above three units in the last place of its largest absolute value; residuals are constant when they are within the rounding of the regression or within three such units of the response. Such a response is centred on its median before the predictors are fitted to it and before the test for spatial structure and, in resolution_profile(), Moran’s I of the cell means, none of which change under a shift. A response whose raw values show their spread through a trend, such as 1e15 plus 1e5 times a predictor plus a spread of 1, is fitted on its raw values; where the OLS residuals of that fit show no spread, the predictors are fitted again to the response less its median, and those residuals are read and scored. On the raw values the rounding of these regressions at 1e15 was larger than the spread: resolution_profile() with predictor_vars scored cp on residuals with a sum of squares about 150 times the spread’s, and gave a cp to a response the predictors fit exactly. A response of one value, values that differ only by their rounding (0.1 beside 0.3 / 3) and the residuals of an exact fit stay constant. Every response whose raw values show their spread, and with predictor_vars whose OLS residuals on the raw values show theirs, gives the numbers it gave, except the residuals of an exact fit that the bound on the raw values took for spread (see the next entry). Values whose spread is between three units in the last place and 1e-12 of their size, such as 3 times (1 + 4 eps times noise), were constant to estimate_sac_range() and now reach the variogram fit, and so do residuals whose spread is between the rounding of the regression and 1e-12 of the response’s size, such as those of 1e3 times a predictor plus 1e-11 times a field, on that predictor. Where the test for cp, which reads the scored rows of the subsample, finds the response constant and the estimate, which reads every row of the layer (of its selection half under select_on = "split") with a value, does not, the warning, print() and select_resolution(criterion = "cp") now say that. They said that the test for cp reads the raw values alone and the estimate’s also reads them centred and scaled, which was untrue of that case.

  • The test for cp in resolution_profile() scored the residuals of some exact fits, where estimate_sac_range() refused the same layer. With predictor_vars, the test read the OLS residuals against 100 .Machine$double.eps^2 times the response’s sum of squares first, and only where that bound found no spread against the rounding of the regression. estimate_sac_range() read the bound on the regression’s rounding only where its floor, a standard deviation of 1e-12 of the response’s largest value, found no spread. lm.fit() and lm() leave more rounding than either bound on some exact fits, and more with more rows. On 800 points, 7 w - 2 w2 on w and w2 left a sum of squares more than twice the first bound, so cp was scored on rounding with no spatialkit_constant_response warning and select_resolution(criterion = "cp") returned 2, while estimate_sac_range() refused the layer as an exact fit by a margin of 4%. Of 100 exact fits on one to three predictors of that layer, at offsets 0 and 1e6, both scored 8 of the 200: the profile gave them a cp, and the estimate ran its test for spatial structure on the rounding and returned “no spatial structure detected”. On a predictor far from 0, such as a northing of 4.5e6 plus the y coordinate, lm() leaves the residuals of an exact fit at about 2 .Machine$double.eps times the size of the terms, which is thousands of times the response, so the floor found spread in them and the estimate ran its test for spatial structure on the rounding. Both functions now read one bound on the residuals alone, whether or not the earlier bounds find spread, taken on the size of the fit’s terms (each row’s absolute intercept plus the absolute products of its predictors and their coefficients) and read on the residuals taken again from the coefficients, which carry the rounding of the response and not that of the fit’s arithmetic. Residuals with a root mean square of at most 10 .Machine$double.eps times that of the terms, or of three units in the last place of the response, are constant, whatever the number of predictors and rows. So the residuals of an exact fit are constant in both: estimate_sac_range() says the predictors explain the response exactly, cp, moran_i and moran_z are NA with the constant-response warning, and select_resolution(criterion = "cp") refuses as it does for any constant response. The same bound refuses Moran’s I of the cell means in determine_optimal_levels(criterion = "morans_i") where it regresses them again about the response’s centre, so the cell means of an exact fit on an integer predictor over 300 cells are no longer scored. Residuals above the bound are scored as before: those of 1e3 w + 1e-11 f on w, 45 .Machine$double.eps times the size of the terms, reach the variogram fit and cp.

  • At a large offset, Moran’s I of the cell means scored the residuals of an exact fit and refused cell means with real spread, so the counts of determine_optimal_levels(criterion = "morans_i") and the moran_z of "morans_i" and "combined" depended on the response’s origin. Where the raw values lost their spread and the response was taken about its centre (1e12 or 1e15 plus a spread of a few units), the residuals of the cell means were tested only against the centred cell means, and the residuals of an exact fit, which are the rounding of the offset, were scored: on 800 points, 30 of 30 random fits a + b w + c w2 at 1e15. Where the cell means were regressed again about the response’s centre, the residuals were refused when within three units in the last place of the raw response, the rounding of a single row, while the rounding and the spread of a mean of n rows are both those of a row over sqrt(n): 1e15 + 1e5 w + f on w gave NA at 20 to 80 cells, and the call fell back to the geometric ranking with a log line that said the cell means differ by rounding alone. The rows are now fitted first, and where their residuals are within the rounding of a row, as resolution_profile() reads its own, I and z are NA. Both passes then test the residuals of the cell means against the rounding of cell means: three units in the last place of the raw response over the square root of each cell’s rows, plus the rounding of the sums each mean is formed from, summed over the cells on the residual degrees of freedom, or the rounding of the regression on the size of the terms of the cell design. The exact fits give NA at offsets 0, 1e6, 1e12 and 1e15, and so do exact fits on cells of 1,200 to 2,200 rows and those on a predictor along which the response at 1e15 changes by a unit in the last place over the layer. The spread above gives the same I and z at 0 and at 1e15, so the counts and moran_z are the same at both offsets. Residuals that the rounding of a row holds (1e15 + 1e5 w + 0.3 f) give NA, and residuals above the bounds are scored as before.

  • A predictor at a large offset was left out of the OLS fits in silence, so rss, cp, Moran’s I and z, the nugget and the range depended on the predictor’s origin. The QR decomposition behind lm.fit() and lm() drops a column whose part orthogonal to the earlier columns is under 1e-7 of its norm, so a predictor whose spread is under about 1e-7 of its size, such as a timestamp in seconds or 1e8 plus a spread of 1, was taken as collinear with the intercept, and the residuals scored were those of the intercept alone. A little below that size the column was kept, but the fit worked on the rounding of the offset, and with a predictor that explains most of the response the numbers moved with the origin by up to 1e-4 of their size. This held in the OLS fit of resolution_profile(), in the regression of the cell means behind moran_i and moran_z there and in determine_optimal_levels(criterion = "morans_i") and "combined", and in the OLS detrending of estimate_sac_range(), which resolution_profile(sac = NULL) reads. On 600 points with a predictor of unit spread, the profile’s rss at its coarsest level was 548 at offset 0 and 2768 at 1e8, and on a clustered layer the estimate’s nugget was 0.010 and 4.01; the warning of determine_optimal_levels() said the cell means were regressed on the cell-mean predictors. A predictor whose centre is more than 1000 times its spread is now taken less its centre before these fits (for the cell means, before they are formed), and a column of times, dates or time differences that estimate_sac_range() is given is read as the numbers lm() reads. The fit of a model with an intercept does not change under a shift of a predictor, so these numbers are now those of the predictor at 0, to rounding. Every other predictor is fitted as it was, to the last bit, and a predictor that is constant, or a linear combination of the others, is still left out. The test for an exact fit still reads the size of the terms of the predictors as given, so the residuals of a response computed from a northing are still constant. The REML detrending of estimate_sac_range() has its own entry below.

  • estimate_sac_range(detrend = "reml") fell back to OLS on a predictor at a large offset, with the reason that the REML fit did not converge. nlme::gls() fails on a predictor such as 1e8 plus a spread of 1, and the estimate warned that “the REML detrending on p did not converge”, detrended by OLS and returned detrend_method "ols" and the range and nugget of the OLS residuals, where the same predictor at 0 gives the REML ones: on 600 points with a predictor of unit spread, a range of 1429 and a nugget of 0 at 1e8 and 1e15, against 1562 and 0.0214 at 0. At 1e5 the REML fit ran on the rounding of the offset and moved in the seventh digit. A predictor whose centre is more than 1000 times its spread is now taken less its centre before the REML fit, as in the OLS detrending, and the test for spatial structure and the test for an exact fit read the same design, the latter with the centres added back, as there. The REML fit of a model with an intercept does not change under a shift of a predictor, so the range and the nugget are now those of the predictor at 0, to rounding. Every other predictor is fitted as it was, to the last bit, and a fit that fails still falls back to OLS with the warning.

  • estimate_sac_range(detrend = "reml") drew its subsample of a lattice by the last bits of the coordinates. The REML fit runs on at most reml_max_n locations and one row a location, drawn by position from the rows in the exact order of their first coordinate. After another unit or origin the first coordinates of one column of a lattice differ in their last bits, so the draw took other rows: on a 40 by 30 lattice at 250 m with reml_max_n = 300 the nugget was 0.206 in EPSG:26915 and in UTM 15N in US feet and 0.241 with the false origin moved by 0.1 m. The rows are now put in order as resolution_profile() puts them, first coordinates within one part in ten million of the extent counting as one column, so the draws take the same points in every unit and origin. Layers on which no two first coordinates come that close get the order, the subsample and the result they got before.

  • estimate_sac_range(detrend = "reml") fell back to OLS on a response at a large offset, with the reason that the REML fit did not converge. nlme::gls() fails on a response at 1e8 plus a spread of 2 as it does on such a predictor: on 300 points the estimate warned, detrended by OLS and returned a range of 1400 and a nugget of 0, where the same response at 0 gives the REML range of 1361 and a nugget of 0.0142, and at 1e7 the REML range moved in the fifth digit. A response whose centre is more than 1000 times its spread is now taken less its centre before the REML fit, as a predictor is, and the centre is added back to the intercept that the test for an exact fit reads. Every other response is fitted as it was, to the last bit.

  • estimate_sac_range() drew its n_max subsample of a lattice by the last bits of the coordinates. The subsample is drawn by position from the rows in the order of their coordinates, and after another unit or origin the first coordinates of one column of a lattice differ in their last bits: on a 40 by 30 lattice at 250 m with n_max = 300 the range was 647 m in EPSG:26915 and in UTM 15N in US feet and 795 m with the false origin moved by 0.1 m. The rows are now put in order by columns of the first coordinate, as in the REML fit above, so the help’s statement that the answer does not depend on the unit or the origin of the coordinates holds for the subsample. Layers on which no two first coordinates come that close get the order, the subsample and the result they got before.

  • estimate_sac_range(detrend = "reml") gave REML in one unit or origin and fell back to OLS in another where the REML range is not identified. On 100 to 150 points of a lattice the REML range can run to 1e8 m and more with a nugget proportion near 1e-6. The likelihood is flat there, and whether nlme::gls() returned a fit or failed on the same rows was set by the last bits of the coordinates it was handed as supplied. On a 20 by 15 lattice at 250 m with reml_max_n = 100, EPSG:26915 gave detrend_method "reml" and a nugget of 0.217, and UTM 15N in US feet and the false origin moved by 0.1 m gave "ols", a nugget of 0.154 and the warning that the REML detrending did not converge. On a 24 by 18 lattice with reml_max_n = 120 it was the other way round. The REML fit now reads the coordinates of the rows it uses centred on the middle of their bounding box, divided by its diagonal and rounded to 2^-30 of it (about a billionth), as the partition hands them to stats::kmeans(), and its range is multiplied back into the layer’s unit. The response and each numeric predictor, whose unit and last bits set the outcome the same way (the response times 1000, or changed by two units in the last place, gave "reml" where the response as given gave "ols"), are read in the same frame of their range, and the coefficients, the variance and the log-likelihoods are taken back to their units. The extent that bounds the starting ranges no longer has a floor of 1 in the layer’s unit, which on a layer under 1 km across in km set other starts than in metres. gls() then gets the same input in every unit and origin, and every configuration tried gives one detrend_method, one warning and one nugget in each. The range is NA on both lattices, before and after. On a 40 by 30 lattice whose REML range is identified, and on the same lattice jittered, the range changed in the sixth digit or less.

  • kriging_adequacy() kriged a response at a large offset on the rounding of the offset. At 1e15 plus a spread of 1 a double holds the values to an eighth, and the replicate means, the kriged and plain cell means and the cross-validation folds were computed on the raw values, so their rounding was of the order of the difference between a kriged and a plain mean. On one layer of 800 points and 36 cells, the same stored values gave shifts beyond 1 in 10 cells at 0 and in 14 at 1e15, and kr_shift moved by up to 1. Where the raw values lose their spread, the response is now centred as estimate_sac_range() centres it before any of these are computed, and the centre is added back to mean and kr_pred alone. kr_shift, the counts print() gives, the replicates’ within-location variance and the cross-validation statistic are those of the same values at 0; mean and kr_pred are in the response’s units, to the precision a double holds them to there. Every response whose raw values show their spread gives the numbers it gave.

  • kriging_adequacy() let the unit, the origin and the row order of the points choose a lattice’s kriging neighbourhoods. On gridded locations several locations are often the same distance from a cell’s centre or a held-out point, and gstat::krige() took its nmax among them by the last bits of the coordinates and by the order of the rows. On a 32 x 24 lattice at 250 m, the same points and cells in US feet or with the false origin moved by 0.1 m moved kr_pred in about half of 48 cells, by up to 0.03, and kr_shift by up to 1; on a 30 x 30 lattice the rows reversed moved kr_pred in 5 of 9 cells and the cross-validation statistic in its fourth digit. The nmax are now chosen by the package’s tie rule, as its other neighbour searches choose them: squared distances within one part in ten million count as equal, and a tie goes to the lower first coordinate, then the lower second. A cell or held-out location whose nmax-th nearest ties with the next is kriged on its own from the locations the rule picks; the test for a cell whose own locations reach beyond its nmax nearest counts with the same tolerance, and the locations added outside it are chosen the same way. The rows are put in order by coordinates, cell ID and response before anything is computed, and a location is still held out under the fold of its first row as given. A location whose rows name more than one cell was given the cell of its first row; it is now no cell’s own, with a warning that gives the count of such locations, and each of its rows still counts in the cell it names. Layers with no tied distances give the same figures, to rounding. A lattice takes longer: one call to gstat per tied cell and held-out location.

  • make_folds() let the unit and the origin of the coordinates choose the block of a lattice point on a block edge, and the neighbours of a buffered split at the buffer distance. A point on the edge two blocks share went to the first block sf::st_intersects() found it in, which was the lower block only while the edge passed through the point exactly; the last bits of the coordinates put it a hair inside one block or the other. On a 37 x 25 lattice at 250 m, 3 x 2 blocks put 469 of 925 rows in another fold with the false origin moved by 0.1 m, and 4 x 3 blocks 448 in UTM 15N in US feet; the selection half of select_on = "split" on a 40 x 30 lattice moved by 786 rows, and with it the rss of resolution_profile(select_on = "split"). A point within a margin of one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the points and the blocks from a block’s edge is now in that block, and a point in two blocks goes to the lower one (for the grid, the cell to its left or below; for supplied blocks, the lower row, as ?make_folds said), in every unit and origin. A point within the same margin of boundary is inside it: lattice points on a boundary drawn through them were read as outside in other units and origins (8 to 50 of 469 points of a lattice clipped to a triangle), so the call warned about them and extended the block region to the points’ bounding box. The block counts behind the leakage advice read an edge point the same way, and cv_block_size_sweep() and the cross-validation functions given these folds score on them. A point outside every supplied block, or outside the cells of a clipped grid, as near two blocks to one part in ten million went to whichever which.min() met first in the last bits of the distances (3 to 10 of 72 such points moved on probe layers in feet, kilometres and moved origins); it now goes to the lower row, and the count of points outside the design and its warning are unchanged. method = "buffered_loo" excluded a neighbour exactly at the buffer distance in one frame and kept it in another: on a 20 x 15 lattice with buffer 500 m, 295 of 300 training sets differed in US feet and 253 with the origin moved. A squared distance within one part in ten million of the buffer’s square now counts as at the buffer, and such neighbours are excluded in every frame, as they were in metres. Layers whose points sit off the block edges and the buffer distance get the same folds as before.

  • make_folds(method = "nndm") and method = "knndm" let the unit and the origin of the coordinates choose the folds of a lattice. On gridded samples many neighbour distances tie. NNDM took each point’s neighbours in the order FNN’s kd-tree or order() gave equidistant ones, broke ties between held-out distances by the exact order of the coordinates, and counted, compared with the target and inserted its distances exactly, so the last bits of the coordinates settled each tie. On a 20 x 15 lattice at 250 m predicted onto a 30 x 25 lattice at 400 m, 195 of the 300 training sets in UTM 15N in US feet differed from those in EPSG:26915, and 234 with the false origin moved by 0.1 m. kNNDM handed Ward’s method and its k-means the coordinates as given and assigned each point to the centre FNN or sf::st_nearest_feature() returned, so on the same layers with k = 5 170 and 290 of the 300 rows were in another fold, and the wasserstein reported was 1191.21, 1223.84 and 1288.05 m. NNDM now orders each point’s neighbours by the package’s tie rule (squared distances within one part in ten million count as equal, a tie goes to the lower column, then the lower second coordinate, then the lower row), and treats distances within that part of each other as equal in its sweep and in its comparisons with the target and with phi. kNNDM’s Ward clustering and k-means read the coordinates centred on the middle of their bounding box, divided by its diagonal and rounded to 2^-30 of it, as the "kmeans" partition does; a point as near two centres to one part in ten million goes to the lower-numbered one, with or without FNN; and of the candidates whose W is within that part of the least, the earliest is returned. The held-out distances and W are in the layer’s unit as before. params$max_ecdf_excess, params$max_ecdf_deficit and params$loo_ecdf_deficit count distances within the same part as equal too: with prediction points beside a lattice, prediction and held-out distances share lengths, and the step between them changed these figures from frame to frame (with the same NNDM folds in all three, max_ecdf_excess 0.42, 0.42 and 0.413 and max_ecdf_deficit 0, 0 and 0.003). params$target_separated, and the out-of-reach warning it can raise on small samples, take a prediction distance within that part of a leave-one-out distance as not shorter. The folds and these figures are now the same in every frame. They need not be the ones any frame gave before: in metres 62 of the 300 NNDM training sets exclude other neighbours at the same distance, with 60670 training rows in all as before, and kNNDM can return another candidate. Layers on which no two distances lie within one part in ten million of each other, such as that lattice jittered by up to 60 m, get the same folds as before. On scattered points such pairs occur by chance: on 800 uniform points 2 of the 800 NNDM training sets changed.

  • assign_features_to_polygons() let the unit and the origin of the coordinates choose the cell of a point on a shared edge, and the row order of polygons_sf choose between polygons its tie-break could not tell apart. A point on the edge two polygons share was in both only while the edge passed through it exactly; the last bits of its coordinates put it a hair inside one or the other, and the bounding-box centres the smallest-area rule compares were compared exactly, so their last bits settled the rest. On a 37 x 25 lattice at 250 m and a 10 x 7 grid of square cells over it, 25 of 925 rows went to another cell in UTM 15N in US feet and 11 with the false origin moved by 0.1 m. With the default predicate, a POINT or MULTIPOINT feature is now in every polygon one of its points lies within a margin of (one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the polygons; in longitude and latitude only while sf::sf_use_s2() is on), the centres are compared within the same margin whatever the predicate and sf::sf_use_s2(), and every row goes to the same cell in every frame, under tie_break = "smallest_area" and "first". Polygons of one area and one bounding-box centre went to the first in the rows of polygons_sf, where ?assign_features_to_polygons said the choice does not depend on their order: the two triangles of a split square, a square and a rhombus of its area about its centre, one polygon under two IDs, in the join by predicate and in the largest-overlap join. The rule now compares the mean of the polygons’ vertices next, lowest, then leftmost, which tells the triangles apart, and a feature whose polygons are equal on every key is given none: its ID is NA, it is counted in attr(, "ties") and listed in its new unresolved, it is kept or dropped as keep_unassigned says, and a warning of class spatialkit_ties_unresolved gives how many such features there are. tie_break = "first" keeps the first polygon in row order. Points off the edges, and features whose candidates differ in area or centre, are assigned as before.

  • kriging_adequacy() kriged points XYZ throughout in three dimensions. gstat::krige() uses every coordinate dimension of its locations, while the variogram is fitted in x and y, so the heights moved every column: on 400 points with heights of 0 to 1000 m, kr_var by 13 percent on average. The points are now read in x and y on every layer, as estimate_sac_range() reads them, and a layer XYZ or XYM throughout gives the result of its XY copy.

  • Four subsamples were drawn by row position, so their results moved with the row order of the input. Each draws, or thins, from the rows in a fixed order now, as estimate_sac_range() and determine_optimal_levels() order their rows before their draws: by coordinates, then the other values that tell rows at one location apart, and for the predictor index of area_of_applicability() by the predictors in turn:

    • summarize_by_cell(deff = "variogram") on a cell of more than deff_max_n points. One cell of 1500 points had a standard error of 0.261 with its rows as given and 0.255 with them reversed, and a cell_weight of 12.8 against 13.4; ..neff_*, ..df_* and ..ci_* moved with them.
